news.title: Intel gets waiver after worries fuzzy US ban on foreign-made robots may hit fabs
paras: Intel, a big chip maker, had robots from Japan that help move parts in its factories. A US ban on foreign‑made robots worried them, so they asked the government for permission. The FCC gave Intel a one‑year waiver so the robots can keep working.

These robots run on set tracks and can be guided by people to move heavy items. They are vital for chip production because they keep the assembly line moving smoothly. Now Intel can finish its updates and keep the plants running safely.

news.title: Video Friday: Quadruped Robot Solves Giant Rubik’s Cube by Itself
paras: A four‑legged robot, called a quadruped, solved a giant Rubik’s Cube all by itself. It used only its feet to turn the colourful sides in just a few minutes, proving that machines can use their bodies like humans do.

This shows how robots can learn to move and touch objects in the same way people do, which could help them tidy rooms, help in factories, or play games. The video comes from IEEE Spectrum’s weekly series about cutting‑edge robots.
news.curious: What other tricks could a robot do if it had human‑like hands?

news.title: Global race to update computers as AI discovers most disruptive hack yet
paras: In 2024, two small bugs in PHP, the language that powers sites like WordPress and Facebook, let most websites risk data theft. The bugs leave behind clues that hackers could read. When the news spread, France, Denmark, Finland and Netherlands pulled sites offline.

PHP Foundation released a fix for every version from the past decade, but earlier the bug was thought too complicated to use. AI now pulls the required timing in milliseconds, making exploitation faster. Site owners must update to protect users and keep sites running.
news.curious: could AI hack even private computers if the same bugs are found there?
news.think: How might this change life in India in ten years?

news.title: Rocket Lab launches 3 'Hawk' satellites to orbit to gather signals intelligence
paras: Rocket Lab fired an Electron rocket from New Zealand to put three Hawk satellites into space. The launch happened at 3.11 a.m. local time. Hawk satellites are small machines that listen to radio signals, like the noises ships and phones make.

If everything goes well, the satellites will orbit 323 miles above Earth and watch for all kinds of radio chatter. Their data helps the U.S. government spot maritime threats and map communication networks, and gives a new way to protect space missions. Soon more powerful AI will analyse what the satellites hear.
news.curious: What will the satellites discover in the dark space between stars?
news.think: What would you test if you had a real lab for a day?

news.title: Space debris: Are we on track for true sustainability? (op-ed)
paras: Commercial space activity is growing fast. Currently about 16,000 satellites orbit Earth, and scientists predict this could rise to 60,000 by 2035. More than 1.2 million debris pieces—small broken bits bigger than 1 cm—also drift in space and could damage satellites.

Space supports almost everything we use, from phones to weather forecasts. If debris strikes satellites, it could shut them down. That’s why cleaning up and expanding space responsibly matters, especially as new satellite constellations and future space data centers are planned.
news.curious: Could a giant cloud of space dust become a new kind of sky?
news.think: Which discovery would help the most people?

news.title: Performing Arts At Hilltop Road
paras: Hilltop Road Primary School dancers, led by Miss Debby and other teachers, practise extra hours and perform before large crowds at Riverside Theatre, the Sydney Opera House, Penrith, and many school events. Members such as Zahraa, who does an impressive split jump, Moroccan‑style smiles and cool moves wow the audience and inspire younger classmates.

Their shows give students confidence, show teamwork, and let them travel across the region. Mrs Baddour and the teachers say the performances boost school pride and keep the dance program growing strong.

news.title: Early Starts & Cozy Camp Fires At The Great Aussie Bush Camp
paras: On the weekend of August 19‑21 I heard about a fun trip to Camp Wombarro, a big outdoor area in the Southern Highlands. Camp is where people learn new skills and play games. The drive there was one hour and forty minutes.

During the camp they tried Flying Fox, a short zip‑line, a Giant Swing that lifted them high, canoeing across water, swimming, and Bush Craft—making tools from leaves. Early each morning everyone woke at six for breakfast, then in the evening listened to a warm campfire before sleeping at ten.

news.title: Mission: Promote Wellness
paras: Everyone faces health problems, from minor colds to serious illnesses, every day. When we feel sick, a small act of care can feel huge. You don’t need a fancy job to help others today by sharing a smile.
A kind word is a tiny gift that keeps giving. It also teaches us empathy. Small deeds grow into big waves of well‑being in the whole community, showing how simple actions can improve many lives.

news.title: Zoo animals enjoy spooktacular Halloween treats
paras: Animals at Whipsnade Zoo are enjoying an early taste of Halloween with some special treats. The lemurs and macaques tucked into carved pumpkins to find sweetcorn and peppers, whilst rhino Hugo enjoyed his usual breakfast of hay and cabbage.

The zoo's keepers been trying to find creative ways to encourage the animals' natural instincts to hunt and explore. Matthew Webb, Head of Zoological Operations at Whipsnade Zoo, said: "As everyone counts down to Halloween, our zookeepers used seasonal squashes to make sure the animals don't miss out on any of the fun"

sport.title: ‘Staying healthy is a real skill’: Mouratoglou explains why Zverev deserves to be No. 1
paras: Patrick Mouratoglou believes Alexander Zverev fully deserves his No. 1 ranking, even if Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz are better players.

Staying healthy, he argues, is “a real skill” that demands sacrifice, and Zverev’s two Grand Slam titles in 2026 marked a mental breakthrough. Alexander Zverev may not be the best player in the world, but his ranking is fully deserved. That is Patrick Mouratoglou’s view, set out in a video on his social media channels in which he argued that staying healthy is a skill in itself, and part of a player’s value.

sport.title: The five players in tennis history to have won the WTA Finals but not a Grand Slam title
paras: Not every WTA Finals champion has also had the same success at Grand Slam tournaments. The WTA Finals have played host to the best WTA players every year since 1972, as they all battle it out to conclude the season.

This has seen the likes of Martina Navratilova and Serena Williams win the title, and more recently Iga Swiatek , Coco Gauff and Elena Rybakina have triumphed at the event. All five of these players have also won multiple Grand Slam titles, but five WTA Finals champions have not won a single major.

sport.title: Tsitsipas, Medvedev pay tribute to Monfils: ‘As respected as someone who has won multiple Grand Slams’
paras: Stefanos Tsitsipas has called Gael Monfils one of his best friends on tour and said that tennis is losing a rare personality as the Frenchman retires. Tsitsipas spoke in Almaty on Friday after reaching the semifinals. “Great friend of mine, one of the best friends that I have on tour.

I’m actually quite sad that tennis is going to lose a person like that,” Tsitsipas said. “You don’t find players on tour like him. He just has this charisma about him that’s very difficult to find.” Tennis needs people that approach life lightheartedly and with humor.
